Tier toggles can hide entire tiers without changing progress.
Show only researched & available removes locked nodes for a cleaner working view.
Tier navigation jumps the camera directly to a chosen tier.
Zoom, fit-view, and interaction-lock controls affect only the graph viewport.
Your visible tiers, availability filter, and viewport are saved per colony.

callout.title: Pin expensive research
callout.body: Pinning a research node adds its complete cost to the Operations Board. With auto-react enabled, the item is removed after the technology is completed.

research-progression.title: Technology Tiers and Progression
research-progression.summary: Highest-tier tracking, cross-tier dependencies, new music, and strategic research order.
research-progression.unlockLabel: Unlocked after completing your first research project

sections.title: Highest Technology Tier
paragraphs: The header displays the highest technology tier you have reached, defined by the highest-tier completed research. It is not an average and does not require every lower-tier node to be complete. Reaching a tier can expand colony capacity and unlock that tier’s soundtrack, but individual recipes and buildings still follow their own research prerequisites.

Some branches reconnect after several tiers. If a seemingly modest material blocks advanced work, trace the required-research edges and use the Almanac to identify its production route instead of assuming that every prerequisite must be located in the same visible tier.

sections.title: What changes when a new tier is reached
bullets: The highest-tier status cell updates.
The music manager unlocks tracks assigned to that tier. The Jukebox can then enable or disable individual unlocked tracks.
Colonist capacity rises with tier progression. Capacity and active reservations are visible in the header.
At later thresholds, additional systems may become accessible. The exact triggering technology or interface event still controls its Guide record.
The accumulated play-time timestamp of each newly reached highest tier is recorded for the Statistics progression chart; it does not impose a time limit.

sections.title: Choosing research intelligently
paragraphs: Prioritize the bottleneck, not merely the numerically highest available node. A new mine can solve raw-material pressure; a processing method can multiply the usefulness of existing ore; a power branch can support future automation; a construction-enabling intermediate may unblock several facilities at once.

Before paying a large research cost, inspect its unlock list and the construction costs of any new building. Research without the materials to build or feed its facility is still valid progress, but it may not solve your immediate production problem.

callout.title: A faint administrative irregularity
callout.body: Tier timestamps are preserved with more care than some personnel records. This has no effect on the research graph. It is, apparently, excellent paperwork.

almanac-basics.title: Resource Almanac
almanac-basics.summary: The book, contents, alphabetical navigation, options, and resource records.
almanac-basics.unlockLabel: Unlocked after opening the Almanac for the first time

sections.title: A complete resource catalogue
paragraphs: The Almanac contains every resource record in the active game data, including materials not yet present in inventory. A resource page can include its category, image, material value, description, chemical formula, historical background, and factual notes. The book is therefore both a production reference and the game’s industrial encyclopedia.

Opening the Almanac from a resource interaction focuses that exact resource. Opening it from the navigation tab uses the configured starting page: cover by default, or Table of Contents if Open on contents page is enabled.

media.alt: An Almanac spread showing a resource page, page navigation, options, and the View Recipes control.
media.caption: Resource identity and production context share one record.

sections.title: Finding a page
bullets: The current Almanac has no free-text resource search. Use the Table of Contents, its alphabet jump controls, or a contextual resource link from Inventory, Production, Research, construction, or a board.
Selecting a Table of Contents row jumps directly to that resource page.
Alphabet buttons scroll the Table of Contents to a starting-letter group; they do not remove other rows. These buttons are omitted in the Chinese locale, where Latin initial grouping is not used.
Cover, Contents, Previous, and Next controls provide deterministic navigation even when realistic page flipping is disabled.
Clicking the resource image opens a larger image view.
Page-flip activity is tracked for Statistics and achievements; it does not unlock recipes.

sections.title: Almanac options
bullets: Open on contents page changes where ordinary Almanac visits begin.
Hide unresearched recipes removes recipes you have not unlocked from recipe lookup.
Hide recipes for unbuilt buildings removes processes assigned to facilities you have not constructed.
These filters simplify the visible lookup; they do not delete recipe knowledge or change the production graph.
Realistic page flipping is a global interface setting. Dragging page edges is optional; navigation buttons remain available.

sections.title: Material value is not currency
paragraphs: Material Value is precomputed from the complete recipe data, not from the recipes researched in this save. No-input outputs and Electricity begin at a base value of 1. Other values propagate through input and fuel costs per unit of output, keep the lowest calculable route, and never fall below 1; an unresolved resource also falls back to 1. Tool cost is not part of that value calculation. The number is useful for broad comparison, but the colony has no market and cannot sell a resource for it.

almanac-recipe-intelligence.title: Almanac Recipe Intelligence
almanac-recipe-intelligence.summary: Producing and consuming recipes, status markings, profitability, and contextual jumps.
almanac-recipe-intelligence.unlockLabel: Unlocked after opening View Recipes in the Almanac

sections.title: Two directions through the graph
paragraphs: View Recipes opens a panel divided into Producing Recipes and Consuming Recipes. Producing recipes have the current resource in outputs. Consuming recipes have it in ordinary inputs. Fuel-only and tool-only relationships are not indexed as consumers in the current implementation, so inspect recipe cards when planning those special costs.

Each recipe card exposes its assigned building, input and output maps, fuel or tool information where applicable, profitability, and research / construction status. The current resource is highlighted inside the card so it remains clear which side of the transformation you are inspecting.

media.alt: The Almanac Recipe Lookup with producing and consuming cards in researched, unresearched, and unbuilt-building states.
media.caption: Status-aware links turn the catalogue into a navigation hub.

sections.title: Action changes by status
bullets: Researched recipe + constructed building: View in Production opens the correct building and selects the recipe.
Researched recipe + unconstructed building: Open in Buildings focuses the facility you must construct.
Unresearched recipe: Open Required Research focuses the technology that unlocks it.
Striped or labeled cards indicate unavailable knowledge rather than missing data.

Can be produced now is a one-iteration affordability hint. It checks recipe research, ordinary inputs, at least one valid fuel option, and at least one required tool. It does not check whether the assigned building is constructed, does not test a manual cooldown, and does not promise that your selected multi-iteration batch is affordable.

sections.title: Using profitability without being misled
paragraphs: Profitability is a stored ratio derived from calculated output value divided by calculated input cost. Its calculation can include proportional tool value and fuel cost, but that theoretical accounting is not the same as the whole-tool ceiling applied to an actual batch. Construction, research, cooldown opportunity, fuel availability, and automation power can still change the practical answer.

The most profitable theoretical recipe may belong to an unbuilt facility or require an unavailable branch. Use the Almanac options to hide such routes when you need an immediately actionable plan, then disable the filters when planning ahead.

operations-board.title: Operations Board
operations-board.summary: Pinning projects, aggregate requirements, live completion, fuel choices, and auto-react.
operations-board.unlockLabel: Unlocked after pinning your first recipe, research, or construction project

sections.title: A cross-screen project list
paragraphs: The Operations Board tracks recipes, research costs, and building-construction costs in one persistent panel. Pin controls appear in those systems. Open or collapse the board with its edge handle or hotkey; collapsing does not remove its items.

At the top, Total Requirements aggregates every pinned item. Each resource compares the combined requirement with live inventory, so producing a material can turn a shortage into a satisfied row without reopening the board.

media.alt: The expanded Operations Board with aggregate resource chips and pinned recipe, research, and building items.
media.caption: One live plan can span the entire colony.

sections.title: Item-specific behavior
bullets: Recipe items allow the iteration count to be increased or decreased. Inputs, outputs, fuel, and tool demand recalculate immediately.
Recipes with fuel options preserve a board-specific selected fuel.
Research items show the exact cost and jump back to the focused research node.
Building items show construction requirements and jump to the focused building card.
A recipe whose facility is not constructed reports that blocker and can redirect you to Buildings.
Unpin removes only that project. Clear All removes every project immediately and does not ask for confirmation. Neither action consumes nor refunds resources.

sections.title: Auto-react to game events
paragraphs: With Auto-react enabled, a pinned research item is removed when that research completes, a construction item is removed when its building is constructed, and a recipe item counts down after matching manual or automated iterations complete. The manual-production path shows a throttled progress or removal notification. Automation applies the same countdown inside its simulation tick but does not emit that board-specific toast, so an automated target can decrease or disappear quietly.
With Auto-react disabled, the board becomes a static reference list. This is useful for recurring production targets or when you want a completed project to remain as a template.

callout.title: The board is a calculator, not a reservation system
callout.body: Pinned requirements do not lock inventory. You can spend those resources elsewhere, and the live status will return to insufficient. The board never executes production or research on its own.

colony-status-deck.title: Colony Status Deck
colony-status-deck.summary: Total output, facilities, tier, colonists, active schemes, blockers, and electricity.

sections.title: Colony progress bank
paragraphs: These values summarize progression; they are not buttons. Detailed breakdowns live in Statistics, Buildings, and Research.
bullets: Total Production is the cumulative number of output units produced, not current inventory. Consumption does not subtract from it.
Buildings shows constructed facility types against the valid building catalogue.
Tier shows the highest completed research tier.

media.alt: The full status deck with progress and operations banks annotated by metric.
media.caption: Current stock, cumulative output, and capacity are different measurements.

sections.title: Colony operations bank
paragraphs: A blocked scheme remains active but cannot advance its current work. Open its building or the Automation Board to identify missing resources or electricity. A stopped scheme is not counted as active and does not reserve colonists.
bullets: Colonists shows available / total. The detail line reports how many are reserved by running manual automation programs.
Active Schemes counts running manual and electronic programs. If any has a blocked reason, the cell reports the number blocked.
Electricity shows current inventory, not per-minute generation or consumption.

sections.title: The central mark
paragraphs: The central Realindustry wordmark is a permanent part of the header. Some late interface sequences may attach meaning or interaction to that mark. If the interface begins behaving as though a decorative element has acquired administrative significance, this Guide recommends professional curiosity and a backup save.

achievements.title: Achievements and Awards
achievements.summary: Categories, rarity, progress, hidden conditions, organizations, and unlock timing.
achievements.unlockLabel: Unlocked after opening Achievements for the first time

sections.title: What an achievement records
paragraphs: Achievements evaluate saved colony statistics and event counters: production totals, specific resources, research, construction, interface use, time patterns, automation, and other milestones. Unlocking an achievement records its identifier permanently in the save and displays an award notification.

The Achievements overlay can be filtered by category and searched. Each card identifies rarity, progress where the condition exposes a measurable target, reward text, and the awarding organization. Locked artwork may be concealed until earned.

media.alt: The Achievements overlay with category filters, progress bars, rarity styling, and one unlocked award.
media.caption: Awards describe colony history; they do not replace progression systems.

sections.title: Important limitations
bullets: Not every condition reveals its exact target before completion.
Progress can update after the relevant production, research, construction, Almanac, menu, or activity counter changes.
An achievement notification does not imply that a recipe, building, or protected archive entry was unlocked unless that system separately says so.
Statistics can help diagnose measurable goals, but hidden or behavioral achievements may require experimentation.

sections.title: Corporate awards language
paragraphs: Award notes are written from the perspective of several organizations, including internal corporate bodies. Their tone is part of the setting. “Performance within expected parameters” is still an achievement, even if whoever wrote it appears constitutionally unable to sound pleased.

statistics-dashboard.title: Statistics Dashboard
statistics-dashboard.summary: Overview, production, activity, tier timing, and automation accounting.
statistics-dashboard.unlockLabel: Unlocked after opening Statistics for the first time

sections.title: Overview tab
paragraphs: Overview summarizes resource keys present in the inventory object, constructed buildings, completed research, total play time, total production, production per hour, the ten largest current stockpiles, technology-tier progression, and automated output. The “unique resources” card counts stored inventory keys, including a key whose amount has later reached zero; it is not necessarily the number of visible positive-amount Inventory cards. Production per hour uses accumulated play time, so it is a long-run historical rate rather than an instantaneous machine rate.

media.alt: Statistics Overview with summary cards, top resources, and technology tier progression.
media.caption: Use the dashboard to understand history, not to control production.

sections.title: Production tab
bullets: Top Produced Resources is cumulative output by resource, not current stock.
Production by Building attributes manual and tracked output to facility types.
Largest Output in One Operation records the largest completed output event. Both manual production and automated Production blocks can raise it.
Gathering Without Tools tracks the early extraction behavior separately.

Total Processed Input Resources is updated only by buildings whose category is recycling. Manual runs add the ordinary input-and-fuel payment map; their separately removed tool is not included. Automated recycling adds every physical requirement, including tools and fuel, but excludes automation Electricity.

Automation counters include output, physical input consumption, electricity consumption, completed Production-block cycles, and configured recipe iterations. One completed block raises cycles by 1 and iterations by that block’s batch count.

sections.title: Activity tab
bullets: Most Used Features is based on tracked button and navigation interactions.
Almanac flips, menu opens, days played, and music tracks heard are historical counters.
Days played uses distinct calendar dates encountered by the save, not total play time divided by 24 hours.
Tracks heard are synchronized from the music manager before opening Statistics so the count reflects the current session.

callout.title: A number can be true in two different ways
callout.body: Inventory answers “How much exists now?” Statistics answers “How much has happened?” The distinction matters whenever a resource is produced and immediately consumed upstream.

notifications-and-idle.title: Notifications and Idle Monitoring
notifications-and-idle.summary: Message types, board updates, cooldown notices, and the inactivity protocol.
notifications-and-idle.unlockLabel: Unlocked after completing your first research project

sections.title: Notification types
paragraphs: A notification is transient; the underlying state is not. If a message disappears, inspect the relevant screen, Guide record, or saved dashboard rather than attempting to reproduce the action merely to read it again.
bullets: Success messages confirm completed actions such as saving, construction, automation installation, or production.
Information messages explain state changes, cooldown completion, unlocks, and non-fatal blockers.
Error messages report missing resources, invalid programs, unavailable facilities, or storage problems.
Achievement and board notifications have dedicated styling and can summarize automatic project progress.
The live notification list keeps at most 24 items. If a burst exceeds that bound, the oldest active items are dropped and the newest are retained.

Most messages remove themselves after their configured duration. A persistent message remains until application logic removes or clears it; the current toast renderer has no user-operated close button.

sections.title: Idle monitoring
paragraphs: At 60 seconds without keyboard, pointer, wheel, scroll, touch, or click activity, the game displays an inactivity warning without sound. At 300 seconds it changes to a severe corporate warning and plays the warning sound. Any monitored interaction clears the warning and resets both thresholds.

Idle monitoring is presentation and lore. It does not delete resources, fail research, or impose a hidden production penalty. Automation may continue according to its own resource and electricity rules while the application remains active.

callout.title: Efficiency protocol
callout.body: The system’s concern about an unattended Director is operationally sincere and emotionally unhelpful. You may take breaks. No Guide record authorizes the colony to object.

settings-and-accessibility.title: Settings and Accessibility
settings-and-accessibility.summary: General behavior, display, graphics, audio, languages, and safe resets.
settings-and-accessibility.unlockLabel: Unlocked after opening the in-game Menu for the first time

sections.title: General and interface settings
bullets: Language can follow the system or use a manually selected supported locale.
Autosave and its interval control the dedicated autosave record.

Notifications can be disabled for success, information, achievement, board, and similar messages sent through the notification provider. Error notifications deliberately bypass this preference. The separate idle-warning overlay is not controlled by this checkbox and still appears at its inactivity thresholds.
Recipe preview tooltips, hotkey hint badges, remembered Buildings position, and tool-efficiency warnings can be toggled independently.
Realistic Almanac page flipping is optional and does not remove button navigation.

sections.title: The in-game Menu shell
paragraphs: Menu contains Resume, Save Game, Load Game, Settings, Jukebox, Main Menu, and Exit. Clicking the dark area outside the menu behaves like Resume. Jukebox also shows the currently reported track beneath its button.

Main Menu and Exit require confirmation. In the Electron build, confirmed Exit asks the desktop shell to quit; in another host it uses the application’s fallback exit action. Opening and closing Menu does not pause, save, or roll back automation by itself.

sections.title: Display and graphics
paragraphs: Windowed, borderless where supported, and fullscreen modes control the shell. Windowed mode can use a chosen resolution. UI scale ranges from a compact to an enlarged interface, and building-grid scale changes how many facility cards fit in the directory.

Graphics quality and feature switches control shaders, WebGL effects, optical effects, realistic ambient particles, ordinary particle effects, animations, and the especially demanding Research Tree effects. Some controls depend on shaders, WebGL, or High quality and are disabled when those prerequisites are off.

media.alt: Settings with General, Display, Graphics, Audio, and Hotkeys tabs visible.
media.caption: Presentation can be reduced without changing simulation rules.

sections.title: Audio and safe use
bullets: Master, music, ambient, UI / sound-effect, and voice volumes are independent. Master scales every other channel.
Production music can be disabled for facility interfaces, left at normal level, or enabled with ducking. The ducking checkbox has no effect while Production Music itself is off.
Building ambient preview on card hover can be disabled.
The in-game music is original and intended to be safe for recorded videos and streams.
Reset restores setting defaults after confirmation. It is not the same action as resetting a save slot.

jukebox-and-audio.title: Jukebox and Dynamic Music
jukebox-and-audio.summary: Tier-based track unlocks, disabling tracks, production behavior, and heard-track statistics.
jukebox-and-audio.unlockLabel: Unlocked with the in-game Menu record

sections.title: Technology unlocks the soundtrack
paragraphs: Music is grouped by technology tier. Reaching a new highest tier unlocks its associated tracks in the active music manager. The Jukebox lists available tracks and can disable individual songs without lowering overall music volume.
Disabled tracks remain unlocked and can be restored later. A save keeps its disabled-track list, while general volume settings are application preferences.

sections.title: Music in production
bullets: Production Music determines whether the soundtrack continues while a facility interface is open.
Ducking reduces music volume substantially in production rather than stopping playback.
Ambient machinery and UI effects use separate volume channels.
Assistant transmissions and other voiced material use the voice channel.
Statistics records distinct tracks heard. It is not the same count as tracks unlocked or enabled.

sections.title: Missing a newly unlocked track
paragraphs: Check the Jukebox’s enabled state, music volume, master volume, and whether production music is disabled. Track selection remains dynamic; unlocking a tier expands the pool but does not guarantee that one exact track plays immediately.

automation-foundations.title: Automation Foundations
automation-foundations.summary: Building-local schemes, manual crews, later electronic cores, and operating modes.
automation-foundations.unlockLabel: Unlocked after opening your first production interface

sections.title: Automation is local to each building
paragraphs: Automation means a saved executable scheme for one constructed facility. A building can hold a manual scheme from the beginning, and later can also hold an electronic scheme, core installation, upgrades, runtime tasks, selected mode, and history contribution. A program configured in one building cannot run a recipe assigned to another building.

Automation repeats recipe work over time instead of executing instantly. Physical inputs, selected fuel, and whole tools are removed when a Production block completes. Electronic Production blocks also remove their calculated Electricity. Outputs enter the same live inventory used by manual production and every other program.

media.alt: A production building’s automation console showing electronic and manual modes, core installation, program controls, and upgrades.
media.caption: Automation belongs to the facility whose recipes it executes.

sections.title: Two modes, one building
bullets: Colonist Automation is available through the manual scheme controls in a production building. It does not require Building Automation research or an installed electronic core.

Electronic Automation is the later core-based layer unlocked by Building Automation research. It requires an installed automation core in that building and consumes electricity while Production blocks operate.
A building cannot run its electronic and manual program simultaneously. Stop the active mode before starting the other.
Programs remain saved while stopped. Stopping clears active runtime tasks and reservations but does not delete the graph.
Ordinary manual Produce remains a separate action. A running program does not prevent you from viewing the production interface, but competing for the same inventory can create blockers.

sections.title: Installing an electronic core
steps: Research Building Automation.
Open an operational building and locate its automation console.
Inspect the building-specific installation cost.
Install Automation Core. The complete cost is consumed once for that building.
Configure and validate an Electronic scheme before starting it.

callout.title: Construction is not installation
callout.body: Building the facility, researching automation, and installing its core are three separate gates. An installed core also does not make an empty or invalid program run.

sections.title: Exact core installation cost
paragraphs: Let t be the building Technology Level clamped from 0 through 10. Installing that building’s electronic core costs the following whole units: Copper Wire = ceiling(30 + t³), Steel Gear = ceiling(5 + t²), Steel Plate = ceiling(4 + t^1.8), Electronic Circuit = ceiling(2 + t^1.5), and Motor = ceiling(2 + t^1.5). The formula is evaluated separately for every building; installing one core does not discount the next.

automation-program-editor.title: Automation Program Editor
automation-program-editor.summary: Creating graphs, connecting ports, checking, autosaving, clipboard actions, and starting schemes.
automation-program-editor.unlockLabel: Unlocked after opening a manual or electronic scheme editor

sections.title: A scheme is an executable graph
paragraphs: Drag a block to the canvas or click it in the palette, configure its fields, and connect output ports to compatible input ports. Execution begins at the single Start block and follows connections. Position is visual; connections and block data define behavior.

Changes are saved automatically to the building and mode, but a changed graph must be checked again before launch. Check Scheme validates structure and highlights involved nodes or edges. Start Scheme is enabled only when launch requirements are satisfied.

media.alt: The automation editor with block palette, connected graph, minimap or controls, validation panel, and start lever.
media.caption: Connections, not screen position, define control flow.

sections.title: Editor controls
bullets: Ctrl + drag performs area selection.
Ctrl+A selects all. Ctrl+C, Ctrl+X, Ctrl+V, and Ctrl+D copy, cut, paste, and duplicate selected fragments.
Ctrl+Z undoes; Ctrl+Shift+Z or Ctrl+Y redoes.
Delete removes selected blocks or edges. Escape clears selection.
Double-click a connection to insert a reroute point; right-click a connection to remove it.
Snap to grid changes placement assistance only.
Clear removes the editable scheme after the relevant interaction; copy a reusable graph first if needed.

sections.title: Copying between buildings and modes
paragraphs: Copy Scheme stores the complete graph in a persistent local scheme clipboard. Paste Scheme replaces the target editor’s entire graph; it is not an append operation. Unsupported block types are omitted for the target mode, electronic Production blocks beyond the current slot limit are omitted, manual error edges are removed, iteration counts are clamped, and a Production block whose saved recipe does not belong to the target building falls back to that building’s first available recipe and first fuel choice.

Selection copy/paste is separate. It stores selected blocks plus only the edges whose two endpoints are selected, then appends a new fragment near the camera center. Pasted blocks receive new identifiers. If the target electronic program lacks free Production slots, excess selected Production blocks and their now-invalid edges are skipped while other accepted blocks can still be pasted.
A copied graph is a design, not live runtime state. Progress, blocked resources, barrier arrivals, and current tasks are not a portable production queue.

callout.title: Build one valid pass before a repeating graph
callout.body: Start → Production → End is the smallest one-pass scheme. For a finite repeating scheme, use Start → Joiner → Production → Loop; connect Loop.body back to Joiner and Loop.exit to End. A manual version must place its required Rest block(s) on the repeating route, normally between Production and Loop. Start has no input port, and two routes cannot share one ordinary input port—this is why the Joiner is necessary.

automation-blocks.title: Automation Blocks and Flow
automation-blocks.summary: Every block type, port semantics, branching, synchronization, loops, errors, and reroutes.
automation-blocks.unlockLabel: Unlocked after adding production logic to an automation scheme

sections.title: Basic and timed blocks
bullets: Block availability depends on mode. Manual schemes use the colonist-safe palette; electronic schemes add electronic-only control blocks after the core system becomes available.
Start: the single entry point. Exactly one is required, and it needs an outgoing connection.
End: terminates a task reaching it. End is optional; omitting it produces a warning because an intentional loop may never terminate.

Production: runs one recipe belonging to the current building for the configured number of iterations and fuel choice. Electronic iterations are limited to 1 + purchased Batch Handler levels; manual iterations range from 1 through 9,999. It has a normal next route; electronic mode can also route an error output when production cannot complete.
Wait: pauses its task for an integer value from 1 through 3,600 seconds, then follows next.
Rest: a fixed five-second pause used by colonist automation and counted toward its mandatory recovery structure.

media.alt: A labeled automation graph demonstrating every block and its ports.
media.caption: Signals travel along directed connections from Start.

sections.title: Decision and repetition
bullets: Condition compares a selected inventory resource with an amount from 0 through 999,999,999 and routes through true or false. Supported comparisons are <, ≤, exact =, ≥, and >. Decimal thresholds are allowed.

Loop accepts a count from 0 through 9,999. It sends execution through body for its configured count, then through exit. A count of 0 always selects body and never selects exit. To repeat earlier work, the body route must return through a Joiner or another legal merge point; Loop does not implicitly jump backward.

The Loop counter counts body selections at the Loop block. In Start → Joiner → Production → Loop with body returning to Joiner, Production runs once before the Loop sees its counter, then once per body selection. A finite Loop value of 3 therefore yields four Production visits before exit.
A finite Loop without an exit is allowed only as a warning-level design issue; decide whether the missing route is truly intentional.
Conditions read inventory when reached. They do not reserve the tested amount, and another branch or building can change inventory afterward.

sections.title: Parallel flow
bullets: Splitter emits one task down every connected branch. It needs at least two branch connections.
Joiner accepts any incoming branch and immediately passes that individual arrival onward. It merges routes geometrically but does not wait for every branch.
Barrier waits until every connected input has received an arrival, consumes one arrival from each input, then emits one next task. Extra arrivals remain queued for the next synchronization.
Splitter output count and Joiner / Barrier input count can be configured from 2 through 8. Reducing a count immediately deletes connections attached to removed numbered ports.
A Production block is single-flight: if another signal reaches the same block while it is already active, the duplicate work is not spawned.

callout.title: Joiner and Barrier are deliberately different
callout.body: Use Joiner when any branch may continue. Use Barrier when all connected branches must rendezvous. Confusing them can multiply downstream work or leave a program waiting forever.

sections.title: Reroute and ports
paragraphs: Reroute is a visual routing node with one connection per side. A task entering from one side exits the other. It does not delay, copy, filter, or synchronize work.

Each ordinary output port and input port accepts only one connection. Splitters and multi-input blocks expose dedicated ports for their fan-out or fan-in. Invalid shared ports are reported during validation.

colonist-automation.title: Colonist Automation
colonist-automation.summary: Capacity, reservations, slower work, worker calculation, mandatory rest, and supported blocks.
colonist-automation.unlockLabel: Unlocked after opening your first production interface

sections.title: Available before electronic cores
paragraphs: Colonist Automation is the manual automation mode. It is not unlocked by Building Automation research and it does not depend on an installed electronic core. Open a constructed building, use the Colonist Automation panel, configure a valid manual scheme, check it, and start it if the colony has enough available colonist capacity.

Saving or starting a manual scheme creates automation state for that building, but it does not count as installing the electronic core. Electronic installation, electronic upgrades, and electronic electricity consumption remain a separate later layer.

sections.title: Colony capacity
paragraphs: Colonist capacity is five people per highest technology tier. A Tier 1 colony has 5 total, Tier 5 has 25, and Tier 10 has 50. The header shows available / total and the number reserved by running manual schemes.
Colonists are reserved by the program, not consumed as resources. Stopping a manual scheme releases its reservation. A saved but stopped scheme uses no capacity.

media.alt: A manual automation scheme with production iteration counts, worker cost, required Rest blocks, and header colonist capacity.
media.caption: Personnel capacity is a shared colony limit.

sections.title: How worker demand is calculated
paragraphs: Each manual Production block requires one colonist for every five configured iterations, rounded upward. A block with 1–5 iterations needs 1 colonist; 6–10 needs 2. Program demand is the sum across Production blocks, not only the branch currently active.

Manual production takes twice the base automation time. In exchange, it does not require the electronic core or electronic power model. It still consumes the recipe’s physical inputs, fuel, and tools.

sections.title: Rest rules
bullets: The program needs at least one Rest block for every two required colonists, rounded upward.
For repeating production routes, enough Rest blocks must appear inside each production cycle—not merely somewhere on an unreachable or one-time side branch.
A shared cyclic component containing several Production blocks is also checked for enough total Rest blocks.
Rest lasts five seconds and cannot be shortened by editing a value.
Manual mode supports Start, End, Production, Wait, Rest, Loop, Splitter, Joiner, and Reroute. Condition and Barrier are electronic-only in the current rules.

callout.title: Capacity planning
callout.body: A larger batch can require another colonist before it improves useful throughput. Compare worker rounding, rest demand, and resource supply instead of always selecting the maximum iterations.

automation-upgrades.title: Automation Cores and Upgrades
automation-upgrades.summary: Installation cost, Speed Governor, Batch Handler, Parallel Controller, scaling, and active levels.
automation-upgrades.unlockLabel: Unlocked after installing your first automation core

sections.title: Upgrades are researched, purchased, and installed per building
paragraphs: Each upgrade family first requires its own research. After that, levels are purchased separately for each installed building core using a building- and level-dependent material cost. Buying an upgrade consumes resources permanently; it is not a colony-wide bonus.

Purchased and active levels are usually the same. Speed is the exception: you can lower its active level down to zero and raise it again up to the purchased level without refunding or repurchasing anything.

media.alt: Automation upgrades showing purchased levels, active Speed level controls, costs, and power consequences.
media.caption: Every throughput increase has a local capacity or energy tradeoff.

sections.title: The three upgrade families
bullets: Speed Governor: every active level multiplies Production-block speed by 1.5, so levels compound rather than add a flat 50 percentage points. The total power rate doubles per active level; per-cycle energy is adjusted because the faster cycle also finishes sooner.
Batch Handler: each purchased level adds one maximum iteration to every electronic Production block. The energy multiplier compounds by ×1.15 for every configured iteration above 1.
Parallel Controller: each purchased level adds one permitted Production block to the electronic scheme. Every additional Production block doubles the power draw of every Production block.

sections.title: Multipliers compound
paragraphs: Speed, larger batches, and additional production blocks affect different parts of the model and can compound into a dramatic electricity requirement. The editor and Automation Board estimate flow using the current graph and active levels. Check those estimates after each upgrade.
An upgraded program can still be slower in practice if it repeatedly blocks on inputs or electricity. Throughput hardware does not generate upstream resources.

callout.title: Purchased does not mean sustainable
callout.body: If a Speed level destabilizes the grid, reduce the active level while expanding power. The material investment remains installed and can be reactivated later.

sections.title: Exact upgrade prices
paragraphs: For each material in an upgrade’s base cost, the next level costs ceiling(base amount × 2^purchasedLevel × (1 + 0.15 × t)), with a minimum of 1 and building tier t clamped from 0 through 10. “Purchased level” is the level before buying: level 0 uses ×1, level 1 uses ×2, level 2 uses ×4, and so on. Reducing active Speed does not reduce the price of its next purchased level.
bullets: Batch Handler base: Steel Gear 4, Aluminum Plate 2, Stainless Steel 2, Electronic Circuit 2, Brass 1, Motor 1.
Parallel Controller base: Steel Gear 5, Lubricant 4, Chrome-Plated Steel 4, Plastic 2, Advanced Circuit 2, Transformer 1, Simple Machine 1.
Speed Governor base: Lubricant 6, Plastic 5, Advanced Circuit 4, Transformer 2, Simple Machine 2, Aluminum Alloy 2, Tool Steel 2, Hydraulic Cylinder 2, Rubber 1, Optical Sensor 1, Processing Unit 1.

sections.title: Exact timing and electronic energy model
paragraphs: A recipe’s unspeeded automated duration is the largest of 5 seconds, its explicit automationTimeSeconds when present (otherwise 5 seconds + 0.75 seconds for every distinct input, output, fuel requirement, and tool requirement + 0.25 seconds per building tier), and its recipe cooldown. Speed divides that duration by 1.5^activeSpeedLevel, with a hard minimum of 1 second. Manual mode ignores electronic Speed and then doubles the unspeeded duration.

Electronic energy consumed when one Production block completes is rounded to two decimals from: building tier × (2 ÷ 1.5)^activeSpeedLevel × 1.15^(iterations − 1) × 2^(electronic Production blocks − 1). The speed term is energy per cycle, not power rate: because the cycle is also 1.5 times faster per level, the resulting power rate doubles per active Speed level. The parallel term uses the number of electronic Production blocks in the scheme, not the number currently executing.

automation-runtime-and-validation.title: Automation Validation and Runtime
automation-runtime-and-validation.summary: Launch checks, blocking, errors, persistence, offline clock safety, and program edits while running.
automation-runtime-and-validation.unlockLabel: Unlocked after starting your first automation scheme

sections.title: Validation before launch
paragraphs: The validator checks graph structure, reachable blocks, port limits, recipe ownership, iteration and production-block limits, fuel validity, manual-mode support, colonist capacity, and rest structure. Errors prevent launch. Warnings identify questionable but potentially intentional graphs, such as no End block.
Validation is structural and state-aware, but it does not promise uninterrupted supply. A valid program can later block because inventory or electricity runs out.

media.alt: An invalid automation scheme with highlighted nodes, edges, and a specific validation message beside a corrected ready state.
media.caption: Fix the first reported structural error, then check again.

sections.title: Blocked production
bullets: A Production task reaches its completion point, checks requirements, and either consumes them and produces output or reports a blocked reason and resource.
Without an electronic error route, the task waits in place and can resume when the missing resource becomes available.
With an electronic error connection, failure routes control through that output instead of holding the task at the Production block.
The header counts blocked schemes; the building console and Automation Board expose more detail.
Conditions do not automatically retry a failed production unless your graph routes back to an appropriate check or loop.

sections.title: Editing a running scheme
paragraphs: Visual-only changes can preserve runtime when the executable graph has not changed. If execution structure changes, active tasks are reset. If a running program becomes invalid, it is saved but stopped so a malformed graph does not continue using stale runtime state.
Starting one mode while the other mode runs in the same building is rejected. Stopping clears active tasks, barrier arrivals, blocked status, and the building’s active-mode marker.

sections.title: Saves and elapsed time
paragraphs: Automation uses a save-relative history clock and normalizes legacy timestamps during loading. This protects history from wall-clock discontinuities and preserves in-progress state. The simulation processes bounded work per tick; changing the computer clock is not a supported way to manufacture resources.

Instantaneous cycles are detected from repeated execution states and blocked with the loopGuard reason; long acyclic zero-duration routes are allowed. Programs can retain thousands of active tasks, with only a high emergency ceiling for runaway exponential fan-out. Timed Production, Wait, or Rest blocks are still recommended in intentional cycles.
Export before experimental edits to a large scheme. A program clipboard preserves design, while a save preserves the design plus installations, upgrades, statistics, history, and runtime state.

automation-board.title: Automation Board and Analytics
automation-board.summary: Live KPIs, cards, graphs, flow modes, time ranges, blockers, and building breakdowns.
automation-board.unlockLabel: Unlocked after opening the Automation Board

sections.title: A colony-wide automation view
paragraphs: The Automation Board summarizes active programs across every building. It reports active buildings, recipes or Production blocks, estimated electricity per minute, inputs per minute, outputs per minute, current-cycle details, and blocked states. Use it to find systemic bottlenecks that are difficult to see from one facility console.

The board is a live overlay with card and graph views. Collapsing it preserves settings and history. Its handle can be hidden when the Operations Board is expanded so the two edge panels do not occupy the same interaction space.

media.alt: Automation Board in graph mode with KPIs, output and electricity history, range controls, and a blocked building row.
media.caption: Compare estimated flow with historical results.

sections.title: Cards, graphs, and list modes
bullets: Cards view emphasizes current building and block status.
Graphs view emphasizes recorded output and electricity history.
Buildings list groups active work by facility; Recipes list emphasizes individual production work.
Flipping a card reveals its alternate details without changing the program.
Context actions can open the source building, production recipe, research, or Almanac resource.

sections.title: Gross and net flow
paragraphs: Gross flow displays production and consumption as separate magnitudes. Net flow combines them by resource so surplus and deficit become visible. The option to include automation energy determines whether electricity demand participates in that flow presentation.

Per-minute figures are estimates derived from the executable graph, durations, upgrades, and configured blocks. Historical charts record what actually happened. A resource-starved program can therefore have an attractive estimate and poor observed output.

sections.title: History ranges
bullets: 10m, 1h, 10h, 100h, and 1000h ranges aggregate saved history at suitable buckets.
History snapshots are recorded no more often than once every ten seconds of the save-relative history clock; chart points are not one sample per production cycle.
Short ranges reveal oscillation and recent blockers; long ranges reveal strategic trends.
No History means the system has not yet recorded usable samples for that view, not that the program is necessarily invalid.
Lifetime KPIs remain useful even when a selected chart window contains little activity.

guide-records.title: Using This Guide
guide-records.summary: Record unlocks, unread badges, search, categories, images, and spoiler boundaries.
guide-records.unlockLabel: Available at the start of every assignment

sections.title: Records appear when they become relevant
paragraphs: The Guide is progressive. It begins with orientation and foundational controls, then unlocks records after concrete events: opening a screen for the first time, completing a milestone, pinning a project, installing automation, or reaching a technology threshold. Unlocks are permanent in that save.

A small Guide updated notification appears when one or more records become newly eligible during active play. A single unlock names the record; a batch reports the count. Records already unlocked when a save is loaded do not replay a burst of old unlock notifications. Like other information messages, this toast can be suppressed by the global Notifications preference; the unread badge remains authoritative.

The numbered badge on the GUIDE navigation button counts unlocked records that have not been opened. Opening a record marks only that record as read and decrements the badge. Mark All Read clears the current unread set; records unlocked later will create a new badge.

media.alt: The Guide modal with category rail, search, unread record marks, article index, and content pane.
media.caption: The Guide itself is a saved, progressive system.

sections.title: Finding information
bullets: Search checks record titles, summaries, keywords, headings, paragraphs, bullets, steps, and callouts.
Category filters narrow the index without changing read state.
New records are marked in the index until opened.
Related Records at the end of an article links only to related records you have already unlocked.
Locked records are represented only by a pending count. Their titles and contents stay hidden to avoid revealing later systems.

sections.title: What the Guide will and will not reveal
paragraphs: Operational rules are explicit, including niche costs, rounding, blockers, and graph behavior. Narrative material is deliberately restrained. Restricted archives and recovered media are meant to be discovered in their own interfaces; this Guide explains how those systems work only after the player has reached them, and never publishes solutions or late-game outcomes.

Occasional corporate phrasing, document numbers, or oddly persistent checksums may overlap with the wider fiction. Treat them as atmosphere unless the game itself asks you to verify something. Technical Documentation Division denies that this sentence has ever contained thirteen words fewer.

registry-access.title: Registry Access
registry-access.summary: Finding the Registry, boot sequence, tier access, searching, verification, and spoiler-safe use.
registry-access.unlockLabel: Unlocked after opening the Registry for the first time

sections.title: Accessing the archive
paragraphs: At Technology Tier 5, a subtle Registry affordance becomes available in the central header mark. The first transition is intentionally unlike an ordinary menu notification. After access has been established, opening the Registry starts its own boot and authorization presentation.

The Registry is a separate progressive archive. Technology tier determines which entries are accessible to inspect; successful verification determines which protected entries have been decrypted. Decrypted entry identifiers are saved permanently.

Director-facing copy in this record has been reconstructed from an interface the Director was not originally expected to operate. Several procedural notes remain intentionally redacted: █████████ access chain, ████████ authorization owner, and █████████████ post-verification routing. The remaining instructions are sufficient for safe use of the UI.

media.alt: The Registry index with accessible and locked entries, search, access tier, and one verification panel without a solved code.
media.caption: The Guide explains the archive but never supplies its answers.

sections.title: Index and detail view
bullets: Registry search checks the entry’s internal identifier, category, and raw preview text. It does not search decrypted full content, status labels, translated replacement text, or verification answers.
Accessible means your current tier permits inspection. It does not guarantee that encrypted content is already decrypted.
Locked entries remain unavailable until their access condition is satisfied.
Embedded data, recovered images, or other media belong to the selected entry and may contain details not repeated in the text.
The footer reports connection, integrity, and access level. These are presentation states, not colony electricity or save-health indicators.

sections.title: Verification challenges
paragraphs: A protected entry presents a reference, hint, or contextual clue and a verification field. Answers are compared case-insensitively after trimming leading and trailing whitespace; other punctuation remains significant unless an accepted answer explicitly includes an alternative. Failure leaves the entry encrypted and permits another attempt. Success stores the entry identifier in the save and reveals restored content.

Some references are intentionally connected to real industrial, scientific, historical, or cultural knowledge. Researching the reference is part of the puzzle. The Guide will not print solutions, exact codes, or a sequence of narrative revelations.

callout.title: Keep discovery outside the production checklist
callout.body: Registry entries can deepen the story and may matter to concealed outcomes, but a verification failure never consumes inventory. Back up the save, read closely, and solve at your own pace. ████████ is not a resource cost.

sections.title: A spoiler-safe observation
paragraphs: Several records disagree about what the colony is for. The disagreement is intentional. No single corporate slogan, damaged checksum, or recovered frame should be treated as the whole answer. If an external transmission seems to recognize language used here, note the overlap and continue; the system is more interesting when assembled rather than announced.

demo-evaluation-build.summary: Scope, completion target, feedback, wishlist links, and save expectations in the demo.
demo-evaluation-build.unlockLabel: Available in the demo evaluation build

sections.title: A bounded industrial evaluation
paragraphs: The demo is a deliberately limited build with its own available research, buildings, recipes, resources, narrative material, and completion target. Systems may contain references to the full progression because the interface and Guide share the same industrial language, but unavailable content cannot be reached merely by stockpiling past the demo boundary.

The welcome and victory overlays summarize the evaluation scope. The demo completion event is tied to its stated evaluation objective and presents run statistics, feedback links, community links, and the full-game store page.

sections.title: Save and feedback practice
bullets: Use normal manual slots and autosaves during the evaluation.
Export a save before reporting a progression blocker so the exact state can be reproduced.
The wishlist link opens the official full-game store page; it does not alter the save.
Feedback and community links leave the game through the supported external-navigation path.
A demo victory overlay can be closed; closing it does not erase completion statistics.

sections.title: Interpreting locked Guide records
paragraphs: The Guide shows only records whose systems are relevant and unlocked in the active save. A pending record count is not proof that every corresponding mechanic exists inside the demo. It also avoids using article titles to spoil what the full campaign contains.

diagnostics-and-bottlenecks.title: Bottleneck Diagnostics
diagnostics-and-bottlenecks.summary: A systematic checklist for “cannot produce,” “not unlocking,” and “automation is slow.”
diagnostics-and-bottlenecks.unlockLabel: Unlocked after using Production or Research

sections.title: When manual production will not run
steps: Confirm the recipe is selected and researched for this building.
Confirm the building is constructed and operational.
Check every scaled input for the selected number of iterations.
Check the separate fuel selector and fuel total.
Check the required tool count using ceiling(iterations ÷ durability).
Reduce the amount or use MAX to identify the currently affordable batch.
If it is a gathering recipe, inspect its maximum batch and cooldown timer.

sections.title: When research or construction seems stuck
bullets: Hover the research node to trace prerequisites; a visible higher tier does not bypass an incomplete edge.
Open the node detail and distinguish prerequisite lock from resource cost.
After research, return to Buildings and pay the separate construction cost.
If a recipe is researched but cannot open, use the Almanac status action to find the unconstructed facility.
Pin the target and compare aggregate requirements against live inventory so another project does not spend the same stock unnoticed.

sections.title: When automation underperforms
steps: Check that the correct mode is running and that the other mode is not occupying the building.
Inspect the blocked reason and blocked resource in the console or Automation Board.
Compare estimated inputs per minute with upstream output and current inventory.
Compare electricity demand with generation and stock. Temporarily lower active Speed if needed.
Verify Condition branches, Loop exits, Joiner versus Barrier semantics, and that every repeating manual route contains enough Rest.
Use historical graphs to determine whether the failure is continuous or periodic.
Validate again after graph edits; executable changes reset runtime work.

callout.title: Diagnose one layer at a time
callout.body: Access → affordability → special requirements → timing → automation flow. Skipping directly to a late layer often hides a simple earlier blocker.

sections.title: When the interface is the problem
bullets: Clear search and filters before assuming data is missing.
Restore hidden tiers, unresearched Almanac recipes, or unbuilt-building recipes when planning ahead.
Lower demanding graphics effects if interaction or graph animation is slow.
Increase UI scale if controls are difficult to read, or reduce it if a modal has too little working space.
Export the affected save before resetting settings or testing another build.

sections.title: Built-in diagnostic interfaces
paragraphs: Ctrl+Shift+M (Cmd+Shift+M on macOS) toggles the Resource Monitor during gameplay. It is an Electron diagnostic: while visible it requests fresh process statistics every five seconds and shows main-process heap / RSS / external memory, renderer and GPU process information when supplied, and total / free system memory, CPU count, and platform. In a browser build without the Electron statistics bridge, the shortcut has no visible panel because no stats arrive.

Ctrl+Shift+D toggles the Developer navigation tab. Its save tools export one selected primary, autosave, or numbered-slot record and can import a JSON save directly into the selected target. This is a lower-level operation than Export All / Import Archive and can overwrite the target, so use it only with a separate archive.

The Developer tab also contains Recipe Hierarchy. List view exposes recipe identifiers, inputs, outputs, and buildings; Graph view expands upstream producers and downstream consumers around one selected recipe to the chosen depth; Chain view lists producers and consumers for the selected resource. Search matches recipe name, identifier, or description, while resource and building filters narrow the data independently. This tool reads recipe data and does not execute or unlock anything.

callout.title: Diagnostics are not progression
callout.body: Process memory, raw identifiers, and dependency graphs can explain a defect, but none of these panels changes affordability, research prerequisites, or late-access archive state unless you deliberately import a different save.

briefing.speaker: Dr. Mira Holland
briefing.text: Director, I am Dr. Mira Holland, your technical liaison. Welcome to New Industrial Zone Zero-Eight on Kepler-442b. You may be wondering where your equipment is. Interstellar cargo is expensive. According to the Corporation, sending you was 340 percent cheaper than shipping a container of tools. Your assignment is to build an industrial colony and eventually produce a Hyperdrive Engine. You will need resources, research, and well-organized production chains. Let us begin.

gather-wood.speaker: Dr. Mira Holland
gather-wood.text: Open the Tree Grove. We need raw materials before we can develop the colony.

produce-wood-batch.speaker: Dr. Mira Holland
produce-wood-batch.text: Select “Collect Fallen Branches”, set the amount to x10, and press Produce.

back-from-tree.speaker: Dr. Mira Holland
back-from-tree.text: Good. Return to the Buildings list.

produce-stone-batch.speaker: Dr. Mira Holland
produce-stone-batch.text: Select “Collect Loose Stones”, set the amount to x10, and press Produce.

back-from-stone.speaker: Dr. Mira Holland
back-from-stone.text: That is enough for our first research. Return to the Buildings list.

open-research.speaker: Dr. Mira Holland
open-research.text: Research turns stored resources into permanent new options. Open the Research tab.

start-research.speaker: Dr. Mira Holland
start-research.text: Press Research. The listed resources will be consumed immediately. Once completed, the research permanently unlocks its buildings and recipes.

research-capacity.speaker: Dr. Mira Holland
research-capacity.text: Reaching a new highest research tier increases colony capacity by five colonists. Tier 1 gives you five. The header shows how many are available, how many you have in total, and how many are assigned to running programs.

back-to-buildings.speaker: Dr. Mira Holland
back-to-buildings.text: Basic Crafting is now available. Return to Buildings. Before constructing anything, we will automate one repeated task.

open-automation-building.speaker: Dr. Mira Holland
open-automation-building.text: Open the Tree Grove again. We are going to make wood gathering continue without repeated manual orders.

open-manual-editor.speaker: Dr. Mira Holland
open-manual-editor.text: Every production site supports Colonist Automation from the beginning. It does not require an electronic automation core. Open the editor.

automation-layout.speaker: Dr. Mira Holland
automation-layout.text: Automation is fully customizable within the blocks and limits currently available to you. You can create sequences, loops, pauses, and later much more complex logic. Blocks perform work, but the connections between their ports determine what actually happens. This first cycle is only an example.

build-automation-loop.speaker: Dr. Mira Holland
build-automation-loop.text: Set the Production block to 10 iterations. This assigns two colonists, and one Rest block is enough for both, so the crew is used as efficiently as possible. Build this continuous cycle: Start into Joiner input 1; Joiner into Loop; the Loop block’s loop port into Production; Production into Rest; Rest into Joiner input 2; and the Loop block’s exit port into End. Leave Loops at zero for continuous operation, then press Check Scheme.

start-automation.speaker: Dr. Mira Holland
start-automation.text: The scheme passed validation. Pull the lever to start it.

close-automation-editor.speaker: Dr. Mira Holland
close-automation-editor.text: Your colonists will now gather wood while you work elsewhere. Close the editor.

open-automation-board.speaker: Dr. Mira Holland
open-automation-board.text: Press the "OPEN AUTO" edge button to open the Automation Board. It gives you a colony-wide view of every running scheme.

close-automation-board.speaker: Dr. Mira Holland
close-automation-board.text: This board shows active programs, estimated input and output rates, electricity demand, production history, and blocked schemes. Use it to find problems that are difficult to notice inside one building. When you are ready, collapse the board by pressing its right edge.

hover-hand-crafting.speaker: Dr. Mira Holland
hover-hand-crafting.text: Your research unlocked Hand Crafting. Hover over its card to inspect the construction requirements.

pin-hand-crafting.speaker: Dr. Mira Holland
pin-hand-crafting.text: Pin these requirements to the Operations Board. Pinning a project does not reserve or spend resources. It keeps the live requirements visible while you work elsewhere.

open-operations-board.speaker: Dr. Mira Holland
open-operations-board.text: Press the "OPEN BOARD" edge button to open the Operations Board.

close-operations-board.speaker: Dr. Mira Holland
close-operations-board.text: The board combines requirements from pinned buildings, research, and recipes, then compares the total with your current inventory. With Auto-react enabled, completed projects are removed automatically. Collapse the board by pressing its right edge, then gather what is still missing.

wait-for-construction.speaker: Dr. Mira Holland
wait-for-construction.text: Construct Hand Crafting when you have the required resources. This is your first independent production decision.

almanac.speaker: Dr. Mira Holland
almanac.text: Open the Almanac. It explains resources and recipes, shows where materials are produced and used, and helps trace complete production chains.

open-guide.speaker: Dr. Mira Holland
open-guide.text: For exact rules, advanced automation blocks, formulas, controls, and troubleshooting, open the Guide. It unlocks relevant articles as you encounter new systems, so you can read as much or as little as you need.

conclusion.speaker: Dr. Mira Holland
conclusion.text: You now know how to gather, research, plan, build, and automate. From here, develop the colony toward the Hyperdrive Engine. The Corporation monitors progress. Efficiency is rewarded. Stagnation is... recorded. I will be watching your metrics, Director. Good luck.
